name: Minute intestinal flukes (MIF)

taxonomy.lineage: Platyhelminthes > Trematoda; several genera, especially Heterophyidae
taxonomy.rank_note: Reference groups can include multiple species. Protozoan higher-rank systems differ; the lineage is provided without forcing every clade into a class rank.

morphology: Egg group: small yellow-brown, operculated, usually embryonated eggs; dimensions vary by genus and overlap liver-fluke eggs.
Heterophyes eggs are about 28–30 × 15–17 µm; a group label must not imply a single fixed size or species.

transmission.detail: Typical fish-borne members develop through snail and fish hosts. Metacercariae are ingested with fish and adults release eggs from the intestine.

life_cycle.detail: Typical fish-borne members develop through snail and fish hosts. Metacercariae are ingested with fish and adults release eggs from the intestine.
Small operculated eggs in stool; species identity may require molecular or adult-worm evidence.

hosts: Definitive: humans and other fish-eating vertebrates, depending on species. Intermediate: snail then fish for common heterophyids.
distribution: Several members occur in Southeast Asia; species composition varies locally, including Thai communities.
clinical_significance: Often mild; intestinal infection can produce abdominal pain and diarrhea. The group encompasses species with different clinical behavior.
specimen: Small operculated eggs in stool; species identity may require molecular or adult-worm evidence.
diagnostics: Concentrated stool wet mounts at about 400×; record size using calibrated optics.
Where mixed infections occur, a stool PCR result does not identify every individual egg in its images.
differential_diagnosis: OV, Clonorchis and MIF eggs can overlap substantially.
Use MIF egg as a morphology-group target; do not automatically relabel detections as Haplorchis taichui.
review_status: Source-compiled educational content; not independently clinically validated

annotation_guidance: Record specimen, stage, stain, objective/total magnification, pixel calibration, source image and reviewer certainty.
Native crops of 200–650 pixels do not determine biological size. Retain µm-per-pixel calibration before resizing.
Split training, validation and test data by patient/specimen; keep related crops in the same split.
Keep damaged or ambiguous objects uncertain. Molecular confirmation of a mixed specimen does not assign every pictured object a species.
